content.title: About
content.content: Black rice (also called “forbidden rice”) is a whole‑grain variety with a dark purple hull, rich in antioxidants. The unenriched raw form retains its natural nutrient profile and a characteristic nutty aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black rice contains anthocyanins – the same pigments that give blueberries their color.
It has been traditionally cultivated in Southeast Asia, especially China and Thailand.
Ancient Chinese records called it “forbidden rice” because it was a delicacy reserved for the emperor.
Black rice cooks longer than white rice, usually 40‑50 minutes after soaking.
It is often used in festive dishes and desserts for its striking color and texture.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins help combat free radicals, supporting cellular health.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Black rice provides more iron than most white rice varieties, beneficial for blood formation.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps regulate blood sugar more smoothly compared with high‑glycemic carbs.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to rice.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Like many whole grains, black rice can contain trace amounts of arsenic; a varied diet is recommended.

items.title: Cooking challenges
items.content: Improper cooking may leave grains too firm, making digestion harder.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse and soak the rice 30‑60 minutes, then simmer until tender. Use it in salads, pilafs, risottos, or sweet dishes such as rice pudding.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, refrigerate or freeze.
